name: The biggest day shift
brief:
A trading desk has `n` staff, numbered 0 to `n - 1`, and each works either the day shift or the night shift. Each pair `[a, b]` in `clashes` names two different people who must work different shifts; a pair may repeat. Return the largest number of staff who can work days, or `-1` when no split keeps every clashing pair apart.

Write `max_day_shift(n, clashes)`.

Example. For `n = 5` and `clashes = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4]]`, staff 0 and 2 go on one shift and 1 on the other, and 3 and 4 are split. The most on days is 2 from the first group and 1 from the second, so the answer is 3.
constraints: $1 \le n \le 200{,}000$ staff and at most $250{,}000$ clashes.
$O(n + m)$ time is the target for $m$ clashes. A chain of clashes can be too deep for Python recursion.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Colour each group of linked staff with a breadth-first search, giving each neighbour the other shift. A clash between two people of the same colour means `-1`. Each group can be flipped on its own, so take the larger side of each.

examples.note: Staff 0 and 2 can work days together; one of 3 and 4 joins them.
Three people who all clash cannot be split over two shifts.

tests.call: max_day_shift(200000, [[i, i + 1] for i in range(199999)])
max_day_shift(200000, [[i, i + 100000] for i in range(100000)] + [[i, i + 1] for i in range(0, 99999, 3)])

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. Unlike a plain check that a split exists, the answer is the largest day shift, so each group's two sides must be counted and the larger kept.
notes: A split exists exactly when the clash graph is bipartite, which a two-colouring search finds.
Each group's colours can be swapped without touching the others, so the larger side of every group goes on days.
Each person and each clash is handled a fixed number of times, so the work is $O(n + m)$.

planted.slip: Counting the colour each search starts with, without flipping groups, misses the larger side.
Never checking an already coloured neighbour misses an odd loop of clashes, so `-1` is never returned.
Walking only the staff named in a clash leaves out people with no clash, who can all work days.
Taking the larger colour over the whole desk, not group by group, misses a group whose larger side has the other colour.
